title: Amazon FBA private-label brand in a generic imported category
subindustry: Marketplace private label (home, kitchen, fitness, accessories)
product_service: Own-brand versions of generic goods (e.g., kitchen gadgets, storage, fitness accessories) sourced from overseas factories, sold primarily via Amazon FBA.
target_customer: U.S. Amazon shoppers searching generic keywords.
purchase_motivation: Price, Prime delivery speed, review count; low brand loyalty.
spending_evidence: U.S. retail e-commerce $347.3B in Q3 2026, 17.9% of retail [C, WS06-S029]. Says nothing about obtainable share for a new private label.
representative_operators: Thousands of FBA private-label sellers; no audited small-seller economics found [E]
Amazon aggregators (Thrasio et al.) bought such brands 2019-2022; several later restructured (not re-verified this session) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Unit price x volume on Amazon; Amazon deducts referral fee (mostly 15%) [B, WS06-S002], FBA fulfillment, storage and inbound placement fees [B, WS06-S001], plus advertising (PPC).
direct_costs: Factory cost, freight, customs duties (legacy Section 301 China duties plus 10-12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariff since 2026-07-24 [A, WS06-S006]; de minimis unavailable [A, WS06-S032]), Amazon referral 15% [B, WS06-S002], FBA fees, storage, PPC 10-20% of sales [E], returns.
contribution_profit_note: Gross margin here = after landed COGS and Amazon referral/FBA fees, before PPC. After PPC, contribution typically ~5-20% of revenue for a new seller [E]; on a $25 item that is ~$1.25-$5/unit.
working_capital_note: Pay factory 30% deposit/70% before shipment; 30-60 days ocean transit; 60-120 days of FBA inventory; Amazon disburses roughly biweekly. Cash tied up 3-6 months per turn [E].
sales_cycle: Consumer, instant; but ranking/reviews take months.
repeat_purchase: occasional - most generic goods are one-time purchases
customer_accessibility: Traffic is reachable instantly but only by paying Amazon ads against entrenched sellers.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed broadly available (Alibaba-type factories); quality control is the issue.
competitive_intensity: extreme - low barriers, Chinese direct sellers, Amazon Basics, review-gaming competitors
entry_strategy: Weak: minor product improvement or bundle; easily copied within months.
licenses: Illinois business registration via MyTax Illinois (no fee listed) [A, WS06-S034]; customs bond/broker for formal entries; product-specific (CPSC/FCC/Prop 65) as applicable.
regulatory_barriers: Low to moderate; category gating, IP complaints, new CBP formal/informal entry data requirements since de minimis suspension [A, WS06-S032].
operational_risks: Listing suspension, hijackers, counterfeit complaints, stockouts that kill rank, quality defects, review manipulation by rivals.
financial_risks: Tariff changes mid-transit (four regime changes Feb-Jul 2026 [A/C, WS06-S005, WS06-S007, WS06-S006]), dead inventory, fee creep (FBA +$0.08/unit avg 2026 [B, WS06-S001]), PPC CPC inflation.
founder_expertise: Product research, sourcing/QC, PPC management, Amazon policy.
staffing: Freelance VAs, photographers; one ops hire at ~$1M revenue.
automation_potential: AI for listing copy, keyword research, review mining, PPC bid rules; human needed for sourcing negotiation and QC.
delegation_potential: High in principle (VA-run), but strategy remains founder-dependent.
scalability: Can add SKUs, but each SKU is a fresh competitive fight; profits rarely compound.
expansion: Walmart Marketplace, TikTok Shop, DTC site; brand sale (aggregator market weakened).
roic_note: When it works, inventory can turn 3-4x/yr at 10-20% net, i.e., 30-80% annual return on inventory [E], but loss of rank or a tariff jump wipes out a year's profit.
critical_assumptions: Landed COGS 25-35% of price after tariffs
unanswered_questions: Exact 2026 FBA fee table for small/large standard tiers (Seller Central login-gated)
Whether the reported April 2026 fuel/logistics surcharge is still in force
Distribution of net margins among new private-label sellers (no credible survey retrieved)

title: Done-for-you DOT compliance management for small/mid motor carriers
subindustry: Motor-carrier safety compliance administration (DQ files, Clearinghouse, filings)
product_service: Monthly per-driver/per-unit program: build and maintain driver qualification files (49 CFR 391.51), annual MVR pulls and reviews, medical-card expiry tracking, annual Clearinghouse limited queries (382.701), maintenance-file and annual-inspection tracking, MCS-150/UCR/IRP/IFTA filing calendar, new-entrant safety audit and compliance-review preparation, CSA score monitoring. Optional bundle with drug & alcohol consortium (WS17-002).
target_customer: Owners/office managers of motor carriers with 2-100 power units; Chicago 8-county area has 11,781 such carriers with MCS-150 updated 2024+ (5,288 with 6-100 PU) [A, WS17-S001]; also private fleets (construction 3,325 carriers, utility 824) [A, WS17-S001].
purchase_motivation: Legal mandate (DQ files, Clearinghouse queries, periodic inspections) with fines, failed new-entrant audits, insurance premium pressure from CSA scores, and shipper/broker vetting; small carriers lack staff to track dozens of expiring items.
spending_evidence: Mandate verified [A, WS17-S004, WS17-S005, WS17-S002]; buyer population verified [A, WS17-S001]. Actual outsourced-compliance spend per carrier NOT verified (MISSING) - web search budget exhausted before pricing could be gathered.
representative_operators: J. J. Keller & Associates - national compliance publisher/services provider (size not verified this session) [E]
Foley Services - driver screening/compliance services (not verified) [E]
Many local 'DOT compliance' consultants and insurance-agency-affiliated services (count unknown) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per-driver per-month subscription plus one-time onboarding/file-rebuild and audit-prep fees; pass-through of MVR/state fees.
typical_transaction_value: Hypothesis: $25-$60 per driver per month; a 10-truck/12-driver carrier ~$300-$700/mo; audit-prep projects $500-$2,500 [E - unverified]
direct_costs: Compliance-coordinator labor, MVR and query pass-through fees, compliance software licences, E&O insurance.
contribution_profit_note: If one coordinator ($50-60k loaded, E) handles ~120-200 drivers with good tooling, contribution per coordinator ~$40-90k/yr at assumed prices [E].
working_capital_note: Bill monthly in advance by ACH/card; negligible inventory; receivables minimal if autopay enforced.
sales_cycle: 1-6 weeks for small carriers; faster when triggered by an audit letter, insurance renewal or new authority.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract - monthly; churn driven by carrier failure in freight downturns.
acquisition_channels: Direct mail/email to FMCSA census list (respect TCPA - no autodialed cell calls)
Truck insurance agents and factoring companies (referral partners)
New-authority filings (new entrants needing safety audits)
Ethnic trucking communities/associations in Chicago suburbs
customer_accessibility: High identifiability: every carrier's name, address, fleet size and often email/phone are in the public census [A, WS17-S001]. Winning trust is harder: carriers are bombarded with scam 'compliance' letters.
supplier_accessibility: Confirmed in principle: MVRs, Clearinghouse and filing portals are open to carriers/agents; specific compliance software vendors not evaluated.
competitive_intensity: high - national publishers, telematics platforms adding DQ modules, insurance agencies offering free tools, and many low-cost consultants.
entry_strategy: Hyperlocal, multilingual, fully done-for-you service with an audit-ready guarantee and fixed monthly price; lead with free file audit; bundle consortium + filings; target 6-50 PU carriers too small for in-house safety staff.
licenses: No federal or Illinois licence identified for compliance administration [E - absence not verified]; must avoid legal advice (unauthorized practice of law). E&O insurance advisable. IFTA/IRP filings need carrier power of attorney.
regulatory_barriers: Low barrier to entry; risk of being lumped with deceptive 'FMCSA update' mailers - marketing must be scrupulously non-deceptive.
operational_risks: Missed expiry creates client fines and liability; data security of driver PII; dependence on timely client document submission.
financial_risks: High churn of small carriers during freight recessions (Rush reports freight recession pressure in 2025 [A, WS17-S021]); price competition.
geographic_constraints: Can be delivered remotely nationwide; Chicago gives dense local base.
founder_expertise: Learn FMCSRs Parts 382/391/395/396, filing systems, carrier operations; strong sales.
staffing: First compliance coordinator at ~40-60 clients; sales rep later; bilingual staff valuable.
automation_potential: High: document intake/OCR of med cards and MVRs, expiry tracking, automated reminders, audit-file assembly, CSA monitoring dashboards. Humans still handle client chasing, judgment calls and audits. Runs on ordinary SaaS + modest API costs.
delegation_potential: Good - coordinator roles are standard admin jobs with SOPs.
scalability: Remote delivery allows multi-state growth; ceiling limited by churn and price competition.
expansion: Consortium/C-TPA (WS17-002), IRP/IFTA and title services (WS17-031), maintenance tracking (WS17-009), insurance referral partnerships (WS02 cross-stream).
roic_note: Asset-light; <$15k at risk; returns depend on CAC and churn rather than capital.
critical_assumptions: Small carriers will pay $25-60/driver/month for outsourced compliance
unanswered_questions: Actual market prices of DOT compliance subscriptions in Chicago
Churn rates for small-carrier service contracts
How many of the 11,781 2-100 PU carriers already outsource compliance
failure_modes: Reputation damage from a client fined due to missed item
Founder becomes the only person who understands the rules

title: Independent freight agent under a host brokerage (agent-to-agency path)
subindustry: Freight agent / agency under host broker authority
product_service: Selling and managing truckload freight for shippers under a host broker's MC authority, bond, insurance, credit, carrier vetting and back office; agent keeps a split of gross margin.
target_customer: Same SMB shippers as WS07-001; host brokerages recruiting agents.
purchase_motivation: Shippers: capacity and service. Host broker: agents bring books of business without salary cost.
spending_evidence: Landstar pays agents 7.8% of revenue ($117.7M in Q3 2026) [A, WS07-S011]; 457 Landstar 'Million Dollar Agents' produce 95% of revenue [A, WS07-S012].
representative_operators: Landstar — ~960 independent commission sales agents [A, WS07-S012]
Numerous agent-model brokers (e.g., Trinity Logistics, Allen Lund agent programs — not verified)
revenue_mechanism: Commission = agreed split (commonly 60-80% to agent) of load gross margin [D, WS07-S018], or % of revenue (Landstar avg 7.8%) [A, WS07-S011].
typical_transaction_value: Load ~$2,800 revenue [A, WS07-S011]; gross ~$300-$400; agent share ~$180-$300 per load at 60-70% split [D/E].
direct_costs: Agent's own phone/software/marketing; sometimes desk fees, chargebacks for bad debt or claims per contract [D].
contribution_profit_note: At $1M annual agent revenue and Landstar-like 7.8% of revenue, ~$78k gross commission before agent's own costs [A-derived, WS07-S011]; at $3M, ~$235k [E].
working_capital_note: Host pays carriers and carries receivables/credit risk (Landstar operating subsidiaries contract with customers and assume credit risk [A, WS07-S012]); agent usually paid after shipper pays [E]. Near-zero working capital.
sales_cycle: Same as brokerage: spot quotes days; routing-guide inclusion 1-6 months.
repeat_purchase: recurring — tendered freight from routing-guide shippers
customer_accessibility: As WS07-001 but host's credit, insurance certificates and track record remove part of the credibility wall.
supplier_accessibility: Host provides vetted carrier network and tools [D, WS07-S018].
competitive_intensity: high — agent recruiting is competitive; splits vary; shippers already have many brokers.
entry_strategy: Low-cost validation of whether the founder can sell freight before committing $75k bond and WC; specialise in a lane/vertical; negotiate contract preserving customer ownership/non-solicit terms to allow later conversion to own authority.
licenses: None for agent personally (operates under host authority); host must hold broker authority + $75k security [A, WS07-S001]; agent contract terms (non-compete/non-solicit) [E].
regulatory_barriers: Low. Must avoid acting as unregistered broker outside host relationship (FMCSA broker/bona fide agent guidance) [A, WS07-S006].
operational_risks: Host instability or slow carrier pay damages agent reputation [D, WS07-S018]; fraud still possible but host vetting helps.
financial_risks: Chargebacks for bad debt/claims if contract assigns them; host insolvency could freeze commissions.
founder_expertise: Freight sales and operations; host training partially covers it.
staffing: Solo initially; later sub-agents or assistants paid from commission.
automation_potential: Prospecting, quote prep, tracking emails; host TMS.
delegation_potential: Low-moderate: book lives with the agent; can build an agency office with reps (Landstar's larger agents run multi-person offices) [E].
scalability: Capped by split; real scaling usually means converting to own authority or building a multi-rep agency.
expansion: Convert to own authority (WS07-001) once book exceeds ~$2-3M revenue [E]; add verticals.
roic_note: Capital at risk <$5k; any profit gives ROIC >1,000% — but return is mostly on founder labor.
critical_assumptions: A reputable host will sign an unproven agent with fair split and no punitive non-compete
Founder can generate ~$1M+ annual freight revenue within 18-24 months
Agent is not saddled with bad-debt chargebacks
unanswered_questions: Typical non-solicit/book-ownership terms in agent contracts
Distribution of agent revenue (median, not just Million Dollar Agents)
Survival rate of new agents in first 24 months
failure_modes: Agent cannot build book and quits
Split erodes economics vs own authority

title: Non-medical in-home senior care agency (IDPH-licensed Home Services agency)
subindustry: Non-medical home care (companion, personal care, ADL assistance)
product_service: Hourly and live-in caregivers for older adults: bathing/dressing help, meals, housekeeping, companionship, dementia support; private pay, long-term-care insurance, VA, and Illinois Community Care Program (Medicaid waiver).
target_customer: Seniors 75+ and their adult children; referral sources: hospital discharge planners, senior living, elder-law attorneys, home health agencies.
purchase_motivation: Need-based: safety, avoiding or delaying assisted living/nursing home, family caregiver burnout, post-hospital recovery.
spending_evidence: Home Instead 603 US franchises averaged $2,609,616 gross sales in 2024 (median $2,261,503) and 78,428 client hours (~$33/hr) [B, WS18-S005]; Illinois CCP pays $30.80/hr for in-home service from 1/1/2026 [A, WS18-S020]; aide jobs projected +18% 2025-35 [C, WS18-S021].
representative_operators: Home Instead — 603 franchises, avg $2.6M (mature, median tenure 15+ yrs) [B, WS18-S005]
A Place At Home — 34 operational outlets incl. Illinois 19 (opened 2021) [B, WS18-S006]
Comfort Keepers, Right at Home, Visiting Angels, BrightStar (Item 19 not retrieved)
Addus HomeCare — large Illinois CCP provider (10-K not retrieved)
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate × client hours (private pay typically higher than $30.80 CCP rate); minimum shift lengths; live-in day rates.
typical_transaction_value: ~$30-38/hour; typical client 15-40 hrs/week ≈ $25k-$75k/yr per client [E; Home Instead implied ~$33/hr B, WS18-S005].
direct_costs: Caregiver wages, payroll taxes, workers' comp, overtime, mileage, training.
contribution_profit_note: A Place At Home outlets report gross profit after direct labor of ~42-64% (most 45-55%) [B, WS18-S006]; office staff, recruiting, marketing and insurance consume much of this — assumed operating margin 8-15% at maturity [E].
working_capital_note: Caregivers paid weekly/biweekly; private pay can be billed weekly in advance or on card, but LTC insurance, VA and CCP pay in arrears (assumed 30-60 days) — meaningful payroll float as census grows.
sales_cycle: Days once a family is in crisis; months to build referral-source trust.
repeat_purchase: recurring — ongoing weekly hours until client transitions or dies; average client tenure MISSING.
acquisition_channels: Senior living and independent living communities
Elder-law attorneys, geriatric care managers, financial advisors
Illinois Community Care Program care coordination units
customer_accessibility: Moderate — families search urgently online, but referral sources take months of relationship-building and track record.
supplier_accessibility: Caregiver labor supply is the binding constraint; national shortage widely reported (not quantified here).
competitive_intensity: high — many franchised and independent agencies in Chicagoland; differentiation via caregiver quality and responsiveness.
entry_strategy: Specialize (dementia, hospital-to-home transitions, 24/7 live-in), guarantee fast start (<24h), pay caregivers above market with guaranteed hours; build dense referral network in 2-3 suburbs.
licenses: IDPH Home Services Agency licence required (210 ILCS 55; 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245); Manager Qualification Review; Health Care Worker Background Check Act fingerprinting [A, WS18-S013]. Fee, manager qualifications and worker training hours MISSING. CCP provider contracting with IL Dept on Aging is separate (process MISSING).
regulatory_barriers: Moderate: state licensure and surveys, background checks, wage-and-hour (federal home care overtime rule), Medicaid program compliance if CCP.
operational_risks: Caregiver recruiting/retention, missed shifts, client injury or abuse allegations, 24/7 on-call scheduling.
financial_risks: Wage inflation vs. bill rates; CCP rate fixed by state; payroll float; workers' comp and liability claims.
founder_expertise: Healthcare-adjacent operations, compliance, caregiver recruiting, referral-source sales. No clinical licence needed for non-medical services.
staffing: Qualified agency manager (if founder lacks qualification) and care coordinator from day 1; caregivers per client; scheduler/recruiter by ~$500k revenue.
automation_potential: Scheduling/matching, caregiver recruiting funnels, EVV/time capture, intake and family updates, billing. Care itself is human.
delegation_potential: Strong — commonly run by general managers; standard roles (care manager, scheduler, recruiter).
scalability: Good regional runway: Home Instead units mature to $2-3M+ revenue; multiple territories/branches possible; A Place At Home outlets reached ~$1.5M avg sales by months 37-48 [B, WS18-S006].
expansion: Home care + private-duty nursing (requires Home Nursing licence), senior move management, home modifications referrals, adult day, geriatric care management.
roic_note: Capital at risk ~$60-120k (licensing, insurance, office, 12-18 months of ramp losses, payroll float); yr3-5 profit $100-300k → ~100-250% [E].
critical_assumptions: Private-pay bill rate in Chicago suburbs ≥$34/hr while paying caregivers $18-21/hr
Founder or hired manager can satisfy IDPH manager qualifications
Ramp similar to A Place At Home young outlets (~$500k sales in year 2)
unanswered_questions: IDPH Home Services licence fee, manager qualification and training-hour requirements (77 IAC 245 not retrieved — ilga.gov 503)
Chicago-area private-pay rates and caregiver wages
Operating (not gross) margins of independent agencies
CCP provider contracting process and payment timing
failure_modes: Cannot staff hours sold — reputation collapse
Thin margin if dependent on CCP Medicaid rate
Founder underestimates 24/7 on-call burden and referral-sales time

title: Online CDL Entry-Level Driver Training (ELDT) theory + CDL permit prep (national)
product_service: FMCSA-registered online ELDT theory curriculum (Class A/B, upgrades, hazmat, passenger/school bus) with TPR certification upload, plus CDL permit-test prep; sold B2C and white-labeled to carriers/behind-the-wheel schools.
target_customer: CDL applicants nationally; motor carriers training new drivers; small BTW schools lacking theory content.
purchase_motivation: Federal mandate since Feb 2022: ELDT completion must be in TPR before skills test.
spending_evidence: TPR shows 34,876 drivers trained in Oct 2026 and 2,093,602 since Feb 2022 (~440k/yr) [A, WS09-S023]. Theory price levels MISSING.
representative_operators: 18,384 active registered providers [A, WS09-S023]; >10,000 removed in enforcement since Dec 2025 [C, WS09-S020]
revenue_mechanism: Per-student fee; per-seat B2B licensing to carriers/schools.
direct_costs: LMS hosting, content maintenance, TPR submissions, support, payment fees, ads.
contribution_profit_note: Digital marginal cost near zero; contribution driven by CAC [E].
working_capital_note: Prepaid; B2B net-30 for carriers.
customer_accessibility: Carriers identifiable via FMCSA data; consumers via search (crowded).
supplier_accessibility: Content self-authored against federal curriculum; no supplier dependency.
competitive_intensity: extreme — 18k+ registered providers, many free-with-employment carrier programs.
entry_strategy: Weak; only plausible wedge is multilingual theory + compliance-proof records for small BTW schools facing FMCSA crackdown.
licenses: FMCSA TPR self-registration; state requirements for schools vary (Illinois SOS rules not verified) [A, WS09-S023].
regulatory_barriers: FMCSA enforcement removing non-compliant providers (raises compliance burden but also clears field) [C, WS09-S020].
financial_risks: Commoditized pricing; freight-cycle sensitivity of driver demand.
founder_expertise: FMCSA curriculum, CDL knowledge (founder may need CDL experience for credibility).
automation_potential: High: AI tutors, translation, automated TPR submissions — but equally available to competitors.
expansion: Behind-the-wheel school (WS09-004), hazmat/tanker endorsements, carrier compliance training.
roic_note: Low capital, but CAC likely eats margin.
critical_assumptions: Theory can be differentiated by language/compliance features
unanswered_questions: Market price distribution for ELDT theory
Share of drivers trained free by carriers
Illinois SOS requirements for driver-training schools

title: Small habitational / landlord property insurance niche (Chicago 2-6 flats and small apartment owners)
product_service: Dwelling fire/landlord, small commercial property and liability, umbrella and portfolio policies for small residential investors; evidence of insurance for lender closings.
target_customer: Individual and LLC investors owning 1-50 rental units; property managers; DSCR/bridge lenders and real-estate agents as referral sources.
purchase_motivation: Lenders require evidence of insurance to close/refinance; rising premiums and non-renewals push shopping [E].
spending_evidence: MISSING - Chicago habitational premium data not retrieved; commission rates 15-20% on property per a published carrier schedule [B, WS02-S016].
representative_operators: Local agencies serving investors (unnamed) [E]
revenue_mechanism: Commission on property/liability premium; renewals.
typical_transaction_value: ~$2k-$20k premium per building per year [E]; commission ~$300-$3,000 [E].
direct_costs: Servicing labor, splits, marketing.
contribution_profit_note: Portfolio owners yield multiple policies per relationship [E].
working_capital_note: Direct bill; escrowed premiums paid by lenders reduce non-pay cancellations [E].
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract: annual renewals; investors add buildings over time [E].
acquisition_channels: Lender and title/closing referral partnerships (cross-stream WS01)
Cook County property/ownership public records for outreach
customer_accessibility: Investors identifiable via public records; referral partners concentrate deal flow [E].
supplier_accessibility: Assumed accessible but unconfirmed: a brand-new agency rarely gets direct appointments; realistic routes are aggregators/networks (SIAA claims start-up carrier access 'from day one' [D, WS02-S013]; Smart Choice markets no fees and a commission split until 'Leadership' level [D, WS02-S014]; fees/departure terms anecdotally material [D, WS02-S015]), branch/MGA platforms that recruit start-ups (TWFG passes ~60% of commission income to its agents [A, WS02-S012]) and E&S wholesalers. Illinois-specific aggregator terms MISSING. Older Chicago frame/masonry multi-unit stock often needs E&S markets [E].
entry_strategy: Become the fastest binder for investor closings (24-hour evidence of insurance) and the portfolio specialist for small landlords.
licenses: Illinois resident producer license with Property and Casualty lines: 20 hrs pre-licensing per line (7.5 classroom), General+State Pearson VUE exams per line, $215 state fee per ~2-yr term, age 18+ [A, WS02-S001, WS02-S002, WS02-S003]; agency business-entity license $150 with a designated responsible licensed producer [A, WS02-S003]; carrier appointments (direct or via aggregator/wholesaler); E&O not found as an Illinois statutory mandate but expected by carriers/aggregators (TWFG branches pay their own E&O) [E; A, WS02-S012]; surplus line producer license (surety bond, SLAI membership, 3.5% tax + 0.04% stamping fee) only if placing E&S directly rather than through a licensed wholesaler [A/C, WS02-S004, WS02-S005].
regulatory_barriers: Producer license; possibly surplus lines via wholesaler.
operational_risks: Hard-market capacity shortages; catastrophic/fire claims; vacancy exclusions.
financial_risks: Premium spikes cause non-renewals; carrier exits.
geographic_constraints: Chicago-specific building stock knowledge; expandable to other Midwest metros.
founder_expertise: Property coverage, building valuation, E&S placement.
automation_potential: Fast quote intake from public property data, renewal remarketing; moderate.
expansion: Lender partnerships, property-manager programs, umbrella, eventual habitational program (WS02-016).
critical_assumptions: Referral partners send steady closing flow
unanswered_questions: Chicago small-habitational premium levels and carrier appetite in 2026
Share of Chicago rentals in 2-6 unit buildings

title: Office/admin and accounting-finance contract staffing (clerical/professional, DTLSA-exempt)
subindustry: Office/clerical and accounting & finance temporary/contract staffing
product_service: Contract AP/AR clerks, staff accountants, payroll specialists, admin assistants and customer-service reps on hourly assignments, plus temp-to-hire.
target_customer: Controllers, CFOs and office managers at 20–500-employee Chicago-area companies, nonprofits and professional firms.
purchase_motivation: Month-end/close backlogs, leave coverage, system conversions, vacancy coverage.
spending_evidence: Robert Half contract talent revenue $2.99B in 2025 at 39.0% gross margin [B, WS12-S007]; Kforce FA revenue $98.7M, down 12.3% in 2025 [A, WS12-S009].
representative_operators: Robert Half — contract talent GM 39.0% but segment operating margin -0.8% in 2025 [B, WS12-S007]
Kforce FA — avg bill rate ~$53/hr Q4 2025 [A, WS12-S009]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate on pay rate; conversion fees on temp-to-hire.
typical_transaction_value: ~$35–60/hr billed [E, anchored to Kforce FA ~$53/hr A]; a 3-month assignment ≈ $18–30k billing.
direct_costs: Wages, payroll taxes, low-hazard clerical workers' comp, benefits under ACA thresholds.
contribution_profit_note: ~$10–16 GP/hr → ~$18–30k GP per full-time contractor-year [E]; incumbent RH shows SG&A (recruiter pay, branches) consumes nearly all GP at cycle trough [B, WS12-S007].
working_capital_note: Payroll weekly/biweekly vs net-30; ~$6–10k float per contractor [E]; factoring 1–5% [D, WS12-S017].
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract — repeat orders from same controllers
customer_accessibility: Reachable via standard B2B outreach; incumbents' brands strong.
supplier_accessibility: Clerical candidates plentiful; quality accounting talent tighter [E].
competitive_intensity: high — Robert Half, Accountemps legacy, many boutiques.
entry_strategy: Narrow specialization (e.g., ERP-specific accounting contractors such as NetSuite/Sage Intacct close support) with technically vetted talent.
licenses: IDOL indicates agencies placing only clerical/professional workers may be exempt from DTLSA registration (56 IAC 260) [A, WS12-S004]; if doing direct-hire, IL Private Employment Agency license ($250–500 fee, $5,000 bond) [A, WS12-S015].
regulatory_barriers: Low; standard payroll compliance and IL wage laws.
operational_risks: Contractor quality; client poaching without fees.
financial_risks: Demand contraction: RH and Kforce FA revenues fell in 2025 [A, WS12-S009; B, WS12-S007].
geographic_constraints: Mostly local/hybrid; remote assignments widen reach.
founder_expertise: Must learn accounting roles/ERP skill vetting.
staffing: Recruiter with accounting background by month 6; account managers later.
automation_potential: AI improves matching and admin; but AI/automation directly substitutes for AP/AR/data-entry and admin work — Robert Half's 10-K lists AI substitution as a risk [A, WS12-S008]. Net: high demand-side substitution risk.
scalability: Moderate; local ceiling unless specialized nationally (remote).
expansion: Direct-hire accounting recruiting; fractional controller services (cross-stream WS02).
roic_note: Float modest (~$100–200k at 20 contractors) [E]; ROIC moderate.
critical_assumptions: SMBs will use a new boutique over RH
AI does not shrink entry-level finance/admin temp demand faster than the firm grows
unanswered_questions: Exact 56 IAC 260 exemption scope for clerical/professional agencies
Local bill rates for AP/AR clerks in Chicago 2026
failure_modes: Secular decline in clerical temp demand from automation

title: Obsolete & surplus industrial-automation parts reseller (tested inventory: PLCs, drives, servos)
subindustry: Surplus/obsolete automation and MRO parts resale
product_service: New-surplus and used/tested PLCs, VFDs, HMIs, servo motors/drives, sensors and fluid-power components from discontinued or long-lead lines. Sold with test reports and a warranty via eBay, an own site and directly to plant maintenance departments.
